[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"API Security and OAuth2/OpenID Connect Technical Tutorial"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Modern API Security"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern web applications rely heavily on Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). Securing these endpoints requires robust authorization and authentication mechanisms. OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) have become the industry standard for securing APIs and delegated access."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding OAuth 2.0 vs. OpenID Connect"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework designed to enable a third-party application to obtain limited access to an HTTP service."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that provides authentication and user profile information via JSON Web Tokens (JWT)."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Authorization Code Flow is the most secure grant type for server-side applications. It involves redirecting the user to an authorization server to obtain an authorization code, which is then exchanged for an access token."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=https://api.example.com/callback&scope=openid%20read:data HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once the client receives the authorization code, it makes a POST request to the token endpoint to retrieve the tokens."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=AUTHORIZATION_CODE&redirect_uri=https://api.example.com/callback&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Securing API Endpoints with JWT Validation"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"APIs protect their resources by validating the incoming access token, typically formatted as a JSON Web Token (JWT). The API must verify the token signature, expiration, issuer, and required scopes."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"{
  "iss": "https://auth.example.com/",
  "sub": "1234567890",
  "aud": "https://api.example.com/v1",
  "exp": 1680000000,
  "scope": "read:data write:data"
}"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for API Security"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always enforce HTTPS to protect tokens in transit against interception and man-in-the-middle attacks."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for public clients such as Single Page Applications (SPAs) and mobile apps."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement strict rate limiting and input validation on all API endpoints to prevent brute-force and injection attacks."}]
